proposed_node.title: Coenzyme Q as a mobile electron shuttle
proposed_node.canonical_question: How does coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) move between the respiratory complexes?
proposed_node.summary: Coenzyme Q is a lipid-soluble molecule that diffuses freely within the inner mitochondrial membrane. It collects electrons from Complexes I and II, becoming ubiquinol (QH2), and carries them to Complex III where they are passed to cytochrome c.

core.title: Coenzyme Q as a mobile electron shuttle

sections.heading: What is coenzyme Q?
sections.body: Coenzyme Q, also called ubiquinone or CoQ10, is a small molecule that shuttles electrons along the electron transport chain. Unlike the large protein complexes (I, II, III, and IV) that are fixed structures embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, coenzyme Q is small enough to move freely. Because it has a long hydrophobic tail, it dissolves in the fatty interior of the membrane and can drift laterally from one complex to the next.

sections.heading: Picking up electrons at Complexes I and II
sections.body: Coenzyme Q is the electron acceptor for both Complex I and Complex II. At Complex I, electrons stripped from NADH are passed down an iron-sulfur chain and then transferred to coenzyme Q. At Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), electrons from FADH2 follow a similar path and are also handed off to coenzyme Q. In both cases, accepting two electrons causes coenzyme Q to also pick up two protons from the mitochondrial matrix, converting it from its oxidised form (ubiquinone, Q) to its fully reduced form (ubiquinol, QH2). Carrying protons as well as electrons is important: it means coenzyme Q transports chemical energy in a form that can later contribute to the proton gradient.

sections.heading: How it moves through the membrane
sections.body: Because ubiquinol is lipid-soluble, it does not need a protein channel or carrier to cross the membrane. It simply diffuses laterally through the hydrophobic core of the inner mitochondrial membrane, much the way a small molecule dissolves in oil and drifts through it. The inner membrane is densely packed with protein complexes, so coenzyme Q does not travel far before it encounters Complex III. The high concentration of CoQ in the membrane and its small size make diffusion fast enough to keep the electron transport chain running efficiently.

sections.heading: Delivering electrons to Complex III
sections.body: When ubiquinol (QH2) reaches Complex III (the cytochrome bc1 complex), it donates its electrons through a reaction scheme called the Q cycle. In the Q cycle, QH2 is oxidised back to ubiquinone (Q) in two steps. As this happens, protons are released into the intermembrane space rather than back into the matrix. This proton release adds to the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase. The electrons extracted from QH2 by Complex III are then passed on to cytochrome c, the next mobile carrier in the chain, which carries them to Complex IV.

sections.heading: Why two mobile carriers?
sections.body: The electron transport chain uses two different mobile carriers — coenzyme Q in the membrane and cytochrome c in the intermembrane space — because the chain spans two physical environments. Coenzyme Q is fat-soluble and diffuses inside the membrane, linking Complexes I and II to Complex III. Cytochrome c is water-soluble and diffuses along the surface of the inner membrane in the intermembrane space, linking Complex III to Complex IV. Together they ensure electrons flow through all four complexes without the complexes needing to be physically connected.

rendering.audience_note: Written for a 16-18 learner at introductory level; no prior knowledge of the Q cycle assumed.
